subject.title: Alameda — Measure M (Charter Amendment - Amend and Repeal Outdated Provisions)

text: Proposed City Charter Amendment Ballot Measure Shall the measure amending City Charter Sections 2-1.1, 2-3, 2-10, 3-7(G), 3-14, 7-2(J), 8-2, 8-5, 10-3, 10-6, 10-7, 10-12, 12-4(A) and (B), 14-1, 17-10, 28-2, 28-3 and 28-4, and repealing Sections 12-3(D) and 23-3 to conform to existing practices and amend and repeal outdated provisions be adopted?

The City of Alameda City Charter is the City’s highest level policy and governance document. The Alameda City Council placed this Measure on the November 3 ballot to allow voters to amend numerous sections of the City Charter in order for the Charter language to (i) conform to existing City and City Council practices and (ii) amend and repeal outdated provisions. Sections to be amended include: Section 2-3 would be amended to clarify and conform with the existing practice that certain high-level City employees, such as department heads or comparable executive-level employees, appointed by the City Manager, City Attorney, or City Clerk shall serve at the pleasure of the appointing authority and do not have civil service protection. Also, the amendment to this Section would permit City Council to create classifications that would provide direct support to elected officials and those appointed would also serve at the pleasure of the elected person/appointing authority and not have civil service protection.
Section 2-10 would be amended to clarify that if there is a vacancy in the office of City Attorney, City Manager, or City Clerk, City Council could designate someone to serve in those offices until it makes a permanent appointment. In addition, prior to a vacancy in the office, incumbents in these offices may designate someone to perform the duties if a vacancy in that office were to occur before City Council makes the interim or permanent replacement appointment. If an unexpected vacancy occurs before Council or the incumbent makes the necessary appointment, the Mayor may make the interim appointment pending City Council action.
Section 8-2 would be amended to make clear that only the City Council may authorize the City Attorney to file litigation on behalf of the City.
Section 10-3 would be amended to provide that one member of the City’s Public Utilities Board (which provides oversight of Alameda Municipal Power) must be an electrical, civil, environmental or mechanical engineer, or an engineer with experience in alternative energy.
Section 14-1 would be amended to make clear that the Planning Board’s power is to make recommendations concerning land use, subdivisions and zoning. Section 28-3 would be amended to provide that for the Historical Advisory Board one member shall be a registered architect, one member shall be a State licensed general building contractor and three members shall have an interest in community design.
Other sections remove provisions concer ning the responsibilities of the City Auditor, for example deleting the Auditor’s review of quarterly budget reports with the Mayor and City Manager (the Finance Director provides this review). Other sections, for example, Section 8-5, makes clear that Council action on certain matters may be by ordinance, resolution or motion.
This Measure is an all or none proposition concerning the 17 sections of the Charter referenced in the ballot question. If approved by the voters, this Measure would conform the City Charter to existing City and City Council practices and amend and repeal outdated provisions in the Charter. If the voters do not approve the Measure, all the Charter provisions referenced in this Measure will remain the same. The Measure will take effect if it is approved by a majority of the voters who vote on the Measure.

Alameda’s City Charter is our local constitution. It should be clear, current, and consistent with the way our City government actually operates. Vote YES on this measure to update outdated provisions while preserving public accountability and the basic structure of Alameda government.
Many provisions proposed for amendment were written for another era. The measure removes obsolete dates and transition language, replaces references to agencies that no longer exist, modernizes terminology, and eliminates redundant or inapplicable requirements. These are practical corrections that will make the Charter easier to understand and administer.
The measure also clarifies several important governmental procedures. It allows the City Council, by majority vote, to authorize support staff for elected officials. It establishes workable procedures to maintain continuity when key City offices become vacant. It confirms that decisions to commence, settle, dismiss, or compromise City litigation require Council authorization, rather than leaving those decisions to informal practice.
Other updates modernize qualifications and procedures for City boards. They recognize current fields of engineering and alternative energy on the Public Utilities Board, update Historical Advisory Board qualifications, and remove outdated restrictions that no longer serve a useful purpose. The measure also clarifies financial reporting and auditing responsibilities and conforms Charter language to current City practices.
This measure does not eliminate public meetings or reduce the Council’s responsibility to act openly. Instead, it puts existing practices into the Charter, clarifies who is responsible for important decisions, and removes language that is confusing, obsolete, or inconsistent.
Alameda should not be governed by provisions that remain on the books simply because no one has taken the time to update them. This measure is careful housekeeping—not a restructuring of City government.
Vote YES for a clearer, more modern, and more workable City Charter.

text: "Measure twice, cut once" is a saying worth raising right now as you, the voter, decide the "simple cleanup of outdated language" ballot measure before you. Unfortunately, City Council as a whole did not "measure twice, cut once" -- it deliberated over the 21 charter changes before you in only one meeting (July 7, 2026). On that night, two councilmembers noted that the 2025-2026 Charter Reform subcommittee did their

prior input from the public or the whole Council.
Had there been considerable public input and considerable Council deliberation, the implications of one proposed "cleanup" change would have been better understood: the proposal to remove the word "electors" from Section 10-6 removes citizenship and eligibility-to-vote as requirements to serve on City Hall boards referenced in Sec. 10-6 (i.e. Public Utilities, Planning, Social Services, Library, and Historical Advisory Boards).

Reason 1: the City Council as a whole and the public had not adequately vetted the proposed changes. Reason 2: some are not the simple “cleanup of outdated language and provisions” proponents claim. With respect to Reason 1, City Council as a whole deliberated over the 21 charter changes in only one meeting. On that night, two councilmembers noted that the 2025-2026 Charter Reform subcommittee consisting of Mayor Ashcraft and Vice Mayor Pryor did their work

input from the public or the whole Council.
In contrast, a 2019-2020 Charter Reform subcommittee consisting of Councilmember Daysog and Vice Mayor Knox-White obtained extensive input via meetings with the Council as a whole, the local League of Women Voters, the Alameda Citizens Task Force, and the public, prior to forwarding reform measures voters ultimately approved in November 2020

text:
The opposition calls these Charter amendments “unvetted,” but every change is printed in the full measure for voters to read. The proposal was developed by a Council subcommittee, published with a staff report and full text, debated at an open Council meeting, and then submitted to Alameda voters. Voters—not the Council—make the final decision.
The opposition identifies two policy choices, but neither is hidden.
First, the measure replaces the requirement that board members be “electors” with a clear requirement that they be Alameda residents and at least 18 years old. This allows adult residents who live, work, pay taxes, and contribute to Alameda to be considered for service whether or not they are registered voters. Existing public appointment procedures remain.
Second, the measure does not eliminate or weaken Alameda Municipal Power’s annual audit, rather it codifies current practice; a panel of 5 city staff, including the City Auditor, makes a recommendation to City Council of what 3rd party Auditor to use. This recommendation is done in a public meeting.
Other amendments improve continuity during vacancies, clarify Council authority over City litigation, modernize board qualifications, update obsolete agency references, and repeal transition provisions that expired decades ago. Reasonable people can debate individual changes. But this measure is transparent, limited, and practical.
Vote YES for a clearer, more workable City Charter.
